title: Colonial rule
hook: from the 1700s to the 1900s, much of the Muslim world came under European rule

segments.voice: Yesterday, the libraries, from Cordoba to Cairo to Timbuktu, rooms of books kept open for readers. Your line was: a library in every city. Did you borrow a book? Today the story turns, and it gets harder. Day one thousand nineteen.

A school map, the kind that once hung on classroom walls. Great swaths of it are shaded in a few colors, one for each European empire. Now lay a second map over it: where Muslims lived. From North Africa to the Indian Ocean, from West Africa to the islands of Southeast Asia, much of the second map sits under the colors of the first. Behind every shaded patch are real towns, real mosques, real families who, within a lifetime, found themselves ruled by people from far away. That's a lot to carry in one lesson. So today's lesson is about one thing only: how to tell it. Today: colonial rule.
screen: `A CLASSROOM MAP, SHADED IN COLORS.` → `LAY THE MUSLIM WORLD OVER IT.` → `TODAY: HOW TO TELL IT.`

segments.voice: Over the modern centuries, European powers came to rule a great deal of the Muslim world. The British in India and Egypt. The French in Algeria. The Dutch in the islands we now call Indonesia. The stories differ from place to place, and an honest telling keeps them different. Some of what came was conquest, war and land taken. Some of it was new railways, telegraph lines and schools, built mostly to serve the rulers, and later put to use by the ruled. Borders were drawn by people who would never live inside them. Old institutions, like the endowments we've been meeting, were in some places taken over or redirected. Muslims answered in many ways, and they did not agree with each other. Some took up arms. Some opened new schools. Some worked inside the colonial system and tried to soften it. Some went into exile. Here's one life that refuses a simple telling. Emir Abdelkader led years of armed resistance to the French in Algeria, lost, and was eventually exiled. Later, living in Damascus, he saw mobs turn on the city's Christians, and he and his men took many of them in and sheltered them. A fighter against a European empire, protecting Christians from a Muslim mob. Both true. The Qur'an asks for exactly this kind of honesty. In Pickthall's words: "O ye who believe! Be ye staunch in justice, witnesses for Allah, even though it be against yourselves or (your) parents or (your) kindred." Justice even against your own side. That's the standard for telling colonial history: name the harm plainly, name the people who resisted and those who didn't, and leave nobody out because they spoil the story. Told honestly.
screen: `EUROPEAN EMPIRES ACROSS THE MUSLIM WORLD.` · `CONQUEST, RAILWAYS, BORDERS, SCHOOLS.` · `MUSLIMS ANSWERED IN MANY WAYS.` · `ABDELKADER: FIGHTER AND PROTECTOR.` · then, large: `BE YE STAUNCH IN JUSTICE.`

segments.voice: The practice: learn one country's story honestly, starting with choosing it now. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one Muslim-majority country. Maybe where your family comes from, maybe somewhere you've only seen on the news. Ask yourself three plain questions. Who ruled it, and from where? What did people lose? Who among them resisted, and how? Don't answer yet. Just hold the questions and the place together. If you pray, you can remember the people of that land in your prayer. If not, just let the place stay in mind as you breathe. The bell holds the time.
Colonial rule. The long stretch when European empires ruled much of the Muslim world, a history to be told with justice, even when it's uncomfortable. Today's word.
Your line: told honestly. Today, read one page about the colonial history of the country you chose, from a writer who lived there if you can find one. Day one thousand nineteen.

howItsDone: Muslim communities remember the colonial period in many ways, from national holidays and museums to the stories of grandparents, and Muslim historians and scholars continue to debate how it changed religious life.

fork.setup: you're Emir Abdelkader, exiled in Damascus after years fighting a European empire. a mob turns on the city's Christians. what do you do?
options: stay out of it. they're not your people.
shelter them in your own household.
leave the city until it's over.
fork.reveal: he and his men sheltered many of the city's Christians. a fighter against an empire, and a protector of his Christian neighbors. both true.
